Summary
Data source overview: The BIML Architectural Risk Analysis paper surveys 78 security risks across the full ML lifecycle, groups them by component, introduces a 6-class attack taxonomy, and links each risk to concrete engineering controls and ten high-level security principles (e.g. defence-in-depth, least-privilege, privacy). It also cites seminal empirical studies that quantify the impact of specific defences such as DP-SGD, anomaly filters or Trojan detection.

Inference strategy justification: The source is a broad survey rather than a single empirical study, so moderate inference was applied to (1) extract the canonical causal chains repeatedly emphasised in the text, and (2) distil them into seven representative interventions that an AI-safety practitioner can evaluate quantitatively downstream.

Extraction completeness explanation: 48 nodes (≈1 per 650 words) cover all major causal-interventional pathways the paper discusses: data extraction, poisoning, back-doored transfer, adversarial examples, over-confidence misuse, online-drift, and cross-cutting defence-in-depth. Every node is connected and reusable across the 500 k-document corpus through consistent naming.

Key limitations: The paper offers qualitative rather than systematic quantitative evidence for some controls (e.g. component-level access control), so several validation-evidence nodes rely on medium evidence strength. Some section titles in the original PDF are informal; closest explicit headings were used.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[74]

Instruction-set improvement: Provide explicit minimum / maximum node targets per 1 000 words to reduce ambiguity; supply an edge-type decision tree with examples; request explicit mapping from validation evidence to numbered bibliographic references to simplify traceability.
